hero.name: Adidev Panday
hero.intro: I'm a Woodstock School student from Ludhiana, India, headed for aerospace engineering. I build AI-driven apps, publish research, and spend my spare hours watching my interesting Youtube feed, F1, playing the violin, and playing sports. Below, you will find everything that I'm proud of.

about.heading: About Me
paragraphs: I grew up in Ludhiana, Punjab, and study at Woodstock School, taking HL Physics, Math AA, and Computer Science in the IB Diploma. My focus is aerospace engineering where I hope to learn about aerodynamics & propulsion.

Outside class, I love building things. I've shipped many AI-powered web apps, developed a React Native app to tackle teen drunk-driving in my hometown, and published research on the risks of digital trading. I co-founded my school's AI Club, lead the yearbook as Editor in Chief, and used to play first chair violin in the Advanced Orchestra. I've competed in varsity football and basketball, interned in product development and CAD, and served on the Academic Honesty Council (AHC) & NHS.

Personally I feel drawn to problems that reward not just rigor but also creativity: from modeling 4th-down football decisions with game theory for my Extended Essay to studying how a paper plane's wing generates lift for my IA.

research.title: The Rise of Digital Trading: Accessibility Versus Risk of Financial Ruin
research.journal: International Journal of High School Research (IJHSR), Vol. 8, Issue 12
research.pageNote: Paper begins on page 89 of the issue.
research.abstract: Digital trading platforms like Robinhood, Groww, and Zerodha have made market access a few clicks away for anyone, educated or not. This paper examines that double-edged shift, covering gamification, finfluencers, and the real cost of frictionless trading. Digitization is useful, but for financially illiterate users, it is a trapdoor.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to the IJHSR issue PDF. My paper starts on page 89.

research.title: F1 CAR ON A CEILING?
research.abstract: Four documentaries claim an F1 car could drive upside down in a tunnel. None say how fast. This paper builds a ground-effect model of a 2022 to 2025 car and shows the honest answer is not a speed but a window, from 208 km/h where the car can finally hold its own motion, up to 327 km/h where its floor gets dragged into the ceiling.
research.modalBlurb: You will be redirected to f1onceiling.netlify.app, an interactive version of the paper.

whyAerospace.heading: Why Aerospace?
whyAerospace.subtitle: F1; My Childhood Love
paragraphs: I was three years old in a red toy Formula 1 car before I knew what a car really was, and I have been chasing the same feeling ever since. F1 introduced me to physics: that races are won and lost in how air bends around a machine, that a wing is just an upside-down piece of metal, that seconds are gained and lost through millimeters. This obsession with aerodynamics grew up alongside me.

But aerodynamics is not the full story. Propulsion is what actually currently attracts me to it, ironic right? Thrust perplexes me: how you take stored energy and turn it into controlled, enormous force, how a column of plasma or a breath of burning air can move a body through a sky or past an atmosphere. I think aerodynamics is how a machine survives the unforgiving air but propulsion is how it refuses to be affected by it. That is why I love aerospace.

photos.alt: In a toy F1 car as a toddler

defaultTemplate.opener: I am applying to {school} because its program lines up with where I want to take my aerospace work.
bullets: Add the most specific course, lab, or professor at {school} that matches propulsion, aerodynamics, or aerospace.
Add the most specific student team, facility, or project at {school} worth naming.
Add the personal fit reason, grounded in something already built or done.

princeton.opener: Plan A is MAE at Princeton.
bullets: MAE 426 is rocket and air-breathing propulsion, the syllabus I'd write myself if nobody were grading it, and Professor Edgar Choueiri's EPPDyL has been pushing Hall thrusters since before I was born.
Princeton Rocketry Club's Team Orbital is building toward the 2027 TigerCub launch. That's a deadline I want on my calendar.
I built AirflowNS to watch flows move on a screen, then emailed Professor Hultmark about his high-pressure wind tunnel because I wanted to watch one move for real.

purdue.opener: If propulsion has a home, it's Purdue.
bullets: AAE 439 is combustion instability, taught at the school where Maurice Zucrow wrote the first American university course in rocket and jet propulsion.
Zucrow Labs still runs real test cells, and Propulsion Morpheus fires LOX and methane hot enough to throw Mach diamonds in the plume.
AirflowNS visualizes external flow. Zucrow burns the internal kind. I'd rather learn both ends of the nozzle in the same place.

uiuc.opener: Illinois Space Society builds engines undergrads normally only read about.
bullets: AE 433 is Aerospace Propulsion, AE 434 is Rocket Propulsion, back to back electives that actually say rocket in the title.
The Illinois Space Society's Hybrid Propulsion team runs a 4 kN paraffin and Nytrox hybrid engine out of the old jet-engine test facility at Willard Airport. I want hands on that stand.

I keep circling chamber geometry, injector plates, and regenerative cooling, the stuff that actually drops cost per launch instead of just specific impulse on a spec sheet. That's the problem I want to work on at Illinois.

virginia-tech.opener: Virginia Tech owns a Mach 7 tunnel. I want to stand next to it.
bullets: AOE 4234 is Aerospace Propulsion Systems, and AOE 4604 has me designing, building, and firing an actual booster before I graduate, not just simulating one.
PropEL runs a Mach 7 hypersonic wind tunnel, one of the few university-owned hypersonic tunnels in the country. Most schools show you a diagram. Virginia Tech has the hardware.
My Navier-Stokes solver tops out well below hypersonic. Scramjet combustion at Mach 7 is flow my own code can't touch yet, which is exactly why I want to be in the room when Virginia Tech runs it.

georgia-tech.opener: Georgia Tech runs both ends of propulsion under one roof, and I don't want to pick a side yet.
bullets: AE 4451 is Jet and Rocket Propulsion, taught inside a department that runs the largest aerospace program in the country.

The Ben T. Zinn Combustion Lab fires gas turbines, air-breathing engines, and chemical rockets. The High-Power Electric Propulsion Lab next door holds the largest university vacuum chamber in the nation for plasma thrusters. Chemical fire on one side, ionized gas on the other.
I don't know yet if I belong on the combustion side or the electric side of propulsion, and Georgia Tech is the one school that doesn't make me decide before I've touched both.

mit.opener: MIT is the reach on this list, and I'm applying anyway.
bullets: 16.50 is Aerospace Propulsion, 16.512 is Rocket Propulsion, and both sit a semester apart from an IAP course literally called Aerospace Nuclear Power and Propulsion.
The MIT Rocket Team runs out of the Space Propulsion Lab. I want to be on that team, not just read about it.

16.512 and Princeton's MAE 426 cover almost the same propulsion ground, which tells me this isn't about the name on the sweatshirt. I built AirflowNS and I've been obsessed with F1 since I was three. I'd show up for the problem set either way.

harvard.opener: Harvard doesn't have an aerospace major, so I'm applying for the parts that function like one.
bullets: The S.B. in Mechanical Engineering at SEAS gets me the fluid mechanics underneath aero anyway: Navier-Stokes, vorticity, lift and drag, the same math I first met taping wings onto paper planes.

The Harvard Undergraduate Aerospace Collective built the first student satellite in Harvard's history and is firing Mojave Sphinx, the Ivy League's first student-led liquid bi-propellant rocket. That's the maker culture I want inside.

Five years translating between Ludhiana and Woodstock taught me to think with engineering sitting beside everything else. Harvard lets me take Government and Economics next to fluid dynamics and treat that as the whole point, not a distraction.

uc-berkeley.opener: Berkeley just built the major I'm trying to get into everywhere else.
bullets: AEROENG 143 is Aerospace Propulsion, sitting on top of a fluid mechanics and combustion tradition the university has run for a century, now finally organized into its own aerospace major.
Space Enterprise at Berkeley is a student-run liquid-fuel rocket team built in 2016 with an actual spaceflight goal, not a competition altitude. I want to be on a team aiming that high.

My work keeps circling the same fundamentals: the lift equation, wing surface area, the physics of an engine. I'd rather push those fundamentals somewhere still deciding what it wants to become than somewhere that already decided decades ago.

uc-davis.opener: UC Davis built an aerospace degree that doesn't hide inside mechanical engineering.
bullets: EAE 140 is Rocket Propulsion and EAE 138 is Aircraft Propulsion, both under a prefix, EAE, Aerospace Science and Engineering, that exists as its own department instead of a track bolted onto ME.
EAE 127, Applied Aircraft Aerodynamics, is the course that would actually teach me the parts of AirflowNS I built by trial and error instead of from a textbook.
I taught myself fluid flow by writing a simulator first and reading the theory after. Davis is the rare place where the degree is named for exactly what I've already been doing backward.

uc-irvine.opener: UC Irvine's propulsion course doesn't stop at rockets.
bullets: MAE 112 covers gas turbines, ramjets, scramjets, and rockets in one semester, a wider slice of propulsion than most schools split across three separate electives.
ENGRMAE 136 is Aerodynamics, and the UCI Combustion Lab is where that course's fire and flow actually meet. That's the overlap I want to work in, not just take notes on.
AirflowNS only models external flow. Watching combustion and aerodynamics taught in the same breath at Irvine is the half of the problem my own simulator still can't touch.

uc-san-diego.opener: Triton Rocket Club is trying to be the first university team to reach space, and I want in on that attempt.
bullets: MAE 170, Experimental Techniques, is the course that turns a simulation into a test campaign, which is exactly the gap between what AirflowNS shows me and what I'd actually need to fly something.
SEDS at UCSD already 3D printed a metal rocket engine, the TRI-D, and the Triton Rocket Club is building a 20 foot two-stage rocket with an actual spaceflight target, not a competition ceiling.
I've spent my time so far on code and CAD, not hardware I can hold. A team building toward an actual first, not a leaderboard position, is where I want to make that jump.

ucla.opener: UCLA's rocket team already flew LOx-ethanol to five figures, and I want the next flight.
bullets: MAE 150R is Rocket Propulsion Systems under Professor Karagozian, paired with MAE 150C, Combustion and Energy Systems, back to back propulsion electives with a combustion researcher's name actually on one of them.

Rocket Project at UCLA flew a LOx-ethanol liquid bipropellant rocket past 12,000 feet under Dr. Spearrin, and RISE is the on-ramp for someone like me who hasn't touched liquid propellant hardware yet.
I've built the software side of propulsion: AirflowNS, a Navier-Stokes solver, CAD. UCLA's rocket team is where I'd finally have to make the hardware agree with the simulation.

bath.opener: Bath's propulsion module sits right after its aerodynamics one, back to back.
bullets: ME32014 is Aerodynamics, ME32015 is Aircraft Propulsion, third year modules that run in sequence instead of making me choose a lane.
Team Bath Drones runs real wind tunnel aero testing, and Team Bath Racing Electric puts almost 90 students from mechanical, aerospace, and automotive engineering onto one Formula Student car.
I built AirflowNS alone, at a desk. Testing a drone wing in an actual tunnel with 90 other people who care about the same airflow is the version of that work I haven't gotten to do yet.

bristol.opener: Bristol is the city Brunel built, and its wind tunnels are still proving things he couldn't.
bullets: AENG31102 is Aircraft Propulsion, taught inside a research group that runs its own Aeroacoustic Wind Tunnel, a closed-circuit facility with an anechoic chamber built for exactly this kind of testing.
The Large Low-Speed Wind Tunnel runs an octagonal test section up to 60 metres a second. That's a bigger tunnel than most undergrads ever get near.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel built this city's bridges and ships by testing ideas until they held. I want to learn aerodynamics somewhere that still runs on that instinct.

manchester.opener: Manchester has a hypersonic tunnel and I want to know what that actually sounds like.
bullets: AERO31212 is Aerospace Propulsion, AERO31321 is Aircraft Aerodynamics, both third year MEng Aerospace modules.

The university runs two tunnels in the National Wind Tunnel Facility network, the Hypersonic Tunnel and the Trisonic Tunnel, part of eight tunnels nationwide spanning subsonic to hypersonic. Most of that range I've only read about.

My Navier-Stokes solver works at subsonic speeds I can sanity check by eye. Trisonic and hypersonic flow is the part of the problem I can't simulate my way into yet, which is exactly why I want to stand next to the tunnel that can.

melbourne.opener: ARES has a hundred members and I want to be one of them.
bullets: MCEN90047 is Aerospace Propulsion, with MCEN90008, Fluid Dynamics, as the prerequisite that actually builds the math underneath it.

The Aerospace and Rocket Engineering Society, ARES, builds student high-power sounding rockets with a membership over a hundred students deep. That's a bigger team than most schools' entire aero program.

I've done propulsion mostly solo: a simulator, a research paper, a CAD file. ARES is the first team on this list big enough that I'd actually have to learn to build with other people, not just for them.

michigan.opener: Every Michigan player touches the Go Blue banner before they play. I want a reason to touch it too.
bullets: AEROSP 530 is Gas-Turbine Propulsion, and the Propulsion and Combustion Engineering Laboratory, PACE, run by Professor James Driscoll, houses a model gas turbine combustor with a real GE TAPS injector pressurizable to 10 atmospheres.
That's not a classroom demo. That's hardware running the same injector technology that flies on actual engines.
I taped wings onto paper planes before I knew what lift was. PACE is the kind of lab where I'd finally get to pressurize the question instead of just sketching it.

sheffield.opener: Project Sunride holds the UK's student altitude record, and I want the next one.
bullets: MEC345 is Aero Propulsion, 10 credits covering gas turbines, pulse jets, ramjets, and solid and liquid rocket engines in one module.
Project Sunride built Sunfire II, a 3D printed bipropellant engine that hotfired at 3.4 kilonewtons in 2023, after their rocket Helen set the UK open altitude record at 36,274 feet in 2019.
I want to work somewhere that's already proven it can print an engine and fly it, not just simulate one. Sunride has already done the hard part once. I want to help them do it again.

southampton.opener: Southampton has the biggest wind tunnel at any UK university, and F1 teams use it too.
bullets: SESA2023 is Propulsion, a compulsory second year module, with SESA6075, Aircraft Propulsion, available later for the part of the subject that doesn't fit in year two.
The jet lab runs supersonic ramjet, turbojet, and rocket engine tests, and the wind tunnel is big enough that Formula 1 teams and Olympic athletes test there, not just aerospace undergrads.
F1 aero is where my obsession with propulsion started. A wind tunnel that actual F1 teams use is the closest I've found to testing in the exact room I grew up watching on television.

bocconi.opener: Bocconi is the one school on this list where I'm not applying for propulsion.
bullets: FINANCE 20188 is Quantitative Finance and Derivatives, paired with Probability and Stochastic Calculus, the math underneath every model I'd actually want to build.
BSIC, the Bocconi Students Investment Club, runs a dedicated Quant division doing algorithmic trading, machine learning, and backtesting. That's a student team, not a lecture hall.
GrowwBot already does conversational financial guidance, and Balancify already builds optimization under constraints. Bocconi is where I'd learn to make that math rigorous instead of just functional.

hku-berkeley.opener: I have spent five years living in two places at once, so a degree built out of two does not scare me.
bullets: HKU's Mechanical Engineering programme runs a genuine aerospace specialization track alongside robotics, energy, and materials, inside a four year BEng.
The first half of the degree sits in Hong Kong, the second half at Berkeley, two teaching cultures and two ideas of what counts as a solved problem before I've even graduated.
Translating between Ludhiana and Woodstock for five years already taught me how to be a person in more than one place. This is the engineering version of that same skill.

nus.opener: NUS runs propulsion as its own course, not a unit buried inside thermodynamics.
bullets: ME4231 is Aerodynamics, and ME5309 covers Aircraft Engines and Rocket Propulsion directly, built on ME2135, Intermediate Fluid Mechanics.
AeroNUS designs and builds competition aircraft for Design Build Fly style competitions. NUS SEDS runs alongside it for anyone who wants the space side too.
I built AirflowNS to simulate the fluid mechanics AeroNUS tests for real on a flying airframe. I want to find out where my simulator is wrong.

tu-delft.opener: DARE has flown rockets named Stratos I through III, and I want to help build the fifth.
bullets: AE2230-II is Propulsion and Power, sitting inside a Faculty of Aerospace Engineering that exists as its own faculty, not a department inside something bigger.

DARE, Delft Aerospace Rocket Engineering, built Stratos I through III and is now developing Stratos V, their first attempt at a cryogenic rocket. That's a harder problem than anything in my own build log.
AirflowNS models external flow on a screen. DARE flies the hardware version of that same question. I want to close that gap.

tum.opener: WARR's first rocket is in a museum. I want to help build whatever's next.
bullets: TUM's Chair of Aerodynamics and Fluid Mechanics runs an Aerospace M.Sc. pathway covering propulsion, aeroelastics, and aeroacoustics, the full stack I keep circling on my own.

WARR has run since 1962, over 650 members deep, building hybrid and bi-liquid rockets, satellites, and lunar rovers. Their first hybrid rocket, built in 1974, the first in Germany, is still on permanent display at the Deutsches Museum.
I like teams that keep their old hardware around as a reminder of how far they've come. That's the kind of propulsion culture I want to join, not just admire from the display case.
